title: Numbers, age & quantities
goal: Count things, ask 'how many / how much', give your age, and use ordinals and the special fractions Gujaratis use every day.
intro:
Gujarati numbers from 1 to 100 are each a separate word (see the Numbers chart) — there's no simple 'twenty-one = twenty + one' pattern, so learn them gradually, starting with 1–20 and the tens.

Gujaratis also use special words for fractions — **સવા** (+¼), **સાડા** (+½), **પોણા** (–¼), **દોઢ** (1½), **અઢી** (2½) — for prices, weights and clock times.

phrases.en: How many children do you have?
How much does it come to?
Give me a kilo of tomatoes.
We live on the third floor.

phrases.native: બહુ વધારે છે, થોડું ઓછું કરો.
phrases.roman: bahu vadhāre chhe, thoḍuṃ ochhuṃ karo.
phrases.en: That's too much — reduce it a little.

grammar.title: Numbers with nouns
grammar.body:
Numbers come **before** the noun and don't change. After a number above one, the noun goes into the plural, but in relaxed speech the plural -ઓ is often dropped because the number already shows it: બે છોકરી or બે છોકરીઓ 'two girls'.

Masculine -o nouns and neuter -uṃ nouns must change: બે કેળાં 'two bananas' (કેળું), ત્રણ દીકરા 'three sons' (દીકરો).

To count people, Gujaratis often add the word **જણ** 'person': ચાર જણ 'four people'. 'All four' is **ચારે** or **ચારેય** *chāreya*.

examples.en: one and a half litres of milk

grammar.title: Asking 'how much / how many': કેટલું agrees
grammar.body:
**કેટલું** 'how much' behaves like an adjective and **agrees** with the noun it asks about:

કેટલો (m) — કેટલો સમય? 'how much time?'
કેટલી (f) — કેટલી ખાંડ? 'how much sugar?'
કેટલું (n) — કેટલું પાણી? 'how much water?'
કેટલા (m pl) — કેટલા માણસો? 'how many people?'
કેટલાં (n pl) — કેટલાં કેળાં? 'how many bananas?'

Prices: **આ કેટલાનું છે?** 'How much is this?' (lit. 'of how many is this?').

Age uses -નો/-ની/-નું: હું વીસ વર્ષનો છું 'I am twenty years (old)' — the ending agrees with the speaker's gender.

examples.en: How much tea do you want?

grammar.title: Ordinals and fractions
grammar.body:
The first four ordinals are irregular: **પહેલું, બીજું, ત્રીજું, ચોથું**. From five on, add **-મું** to the number: પાંચમું, સાતમું, દસમું, વીસમું. Ordinals agree like adjectives: પહેલો દિવસ (m) 'the first day', પહેલી વાર (f) 'the first time'.

Fractions: **સવા** adds ¼, **સાડા** adds ½ (from 3 upwards), **પોણા** subtracts ¼. 1½ and 2½ have their own words: **દોઢ**, **અઢી**. So સાડા પાંચ = 5½, પોણા બે = 1¾, સવા સો = 125.

dialogue.title: At the vegetable cart
dialogue.setting: Kavya buys vegetables from a handcart vendor (lāriwālā) outside her building.

lines.speaker: Kavya
lines.en: Bhai, how much are the tomatoes?

lines.speaker: Kavya
lines.en: Give me one and a half kilos. And the potatoes?

lines.speaker: Vendor
lines.en: Thirty a kilo. How many do you want?

lines.speaker: Kavya
lines.native: બે કિલો. બસ, બધા થઈને કેટલા થયા?
lines.roman: be kilo. bas, badhā thaīne keṭlā thayā?
lines.en: Two kilos. That's all — how much is it altogether?

lines.speaker: Vendor
lines.en: Sixty and sixty: a hundred and twenty.

lines.speaker: Kavya
lines.native: લો, એકસો વીસ. થોડાં લીલાં મરચાં આપશો?
lines.roman: lo, ekso vīs. thoḍāṃ līlāṃ marchāṃ āpsho?
lines.en: Here's 120. Could you add a few green chillies?

culture: Vendors traditionally throw in a few green chillies and a bunch of coriander for free — it's normal to ask for them. Prices are quoted 'per kilo' with -e: ચાલીસ રૂપિયે કિલો 'forty rupees a kilo'. Large amounts are counted in **lakhs** (લાખ, 100,000) and **crores** (કરોડ, 10 million), and written 1,00,000 rather than 100,000.
